figures.caption: Figure 1: A) Experimental setup, grid placement, and camera calibration using a ChArUco board. B) Experimental protocol, showing the hand tasks, the elbow postures (flexion–extension) and wrist positions (supination–pronation; 0◦: supination, 180◦: pronation).

Figure 2: Schematic overview of the spinal-inspired SNN and its relationship with the physiological process during motor control. A) A biological representation of the neural pathways that extend from the brain, through the spinal circuits, until reaching the muscle fibers, thereby generating force and joint movements. The illustrations of the human brain, spinal cord, muscle fibers, and neurons were obtained and adapted from Scidraw.io (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3926243, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4966122, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7668290, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3925929, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3925905). B) Computational model inspired by each stage of the process, where spike encoding converts the sEMG envelope into spike trains, loosely analogous to the descending drive to the spinal cord, the SNN models a simplified version of spinal circuits, and the multilayer perceptron (MLP) maps the SNN activity to the joint angles. In this case, the outputs correspond to fifteen hand joint angles. MCP: Metacarpophalangeal joint; PIP: Proximal interphalangeal; DIP: Distal interphalangeal.

Figure 3: Example of the recordings obtained during the experiments, averaged across 23 participants, in the condition with extended elbow and 90◦ wrist posture. (A) Command signal used to drive the virtual hand presented through the Unity interface, which participants were instructed to follow. (B) Joint angles during the 1FP task, including the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb and the proximal interphalangeal joints of the index, middle, ring, and little fingers. (C) 𝑠𝐸𝑀𝐺𝑅𝑀𝑆 (root mean square) from the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) muscle for each hand task, averaged across channels. (D) 𝑠𝐸𝑀𝐺𝑅𝑀𝑆 from the extensor digitorum communis (EDC) muscle for the same tasks. (E–F) 𝑠𝐸𝑀𝐺𝑃𝑆𝐷 (power spectral density) of the FDS and EDC muscles, respectively, estimated with Welch’s method (1 s Hann windows without overlap; 1 Hz frequency resolution). The black line represents the average across channels, while the gray lines correspond to individual sEMG channels. 1FP: one-finger pinch; 2FP: two-finger pinch; FG: full-hand grasp.

Figure 4: Ablation of the physiologically inspired components. Coefficient of determination (𝑅2; top) and Pearson correlation coefficient (𝜌; bottom) of the proposed method (𝑆𝑁𝑁𝑃ℎ𝑦𝑠𝑖𝑜) and its variants: conventional SNN (𝑆𝑁𝑁𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑣), without the heterogeneous second layer (𝑆𝑁𝑁𝑆𝑝𝑘𝐸𝑛𝑑), and with the spike encoder replaced by the adaptive temporal encoder (𝑆𝑁𝑁𝐻𝑒𝑡𝑒𝑀𝑁 ). Values correspond to the median across the 30 conditions for each participant. * denotes statistically significant differences (𝑝 <0.05).

Figure 5: Effect of the amplitude of the spike encoder’s modulating signal (𝜃) on decoding performance in the full-hand grasp (FG) task (wrist at 90◦, elbow extended). (A) Coefficient of determination (𝑅2) and Pearson correlation coefficient (𝜌) as a function of 𝜃, displaying the population’s mean and 95% confidence interval. The relationship between 𝜃 and the spike encoder’s firing rate is depicted in the subfigure (orange line). (B) A comparison of the predictions for 𝜃 values of 50, 300, and 600 with the true signal (index finger angle at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint for a single randomly selected participant). (C) The evolution of the validation L1 loss function (𝐿𝑜𝑠𝑠𝑀𝐴𝐸 , mean absolute error) for each of the three 𝜃 values in a single randomly selected participant during training. * denotes statistically significant differences in 𝑅2 (𝑝 <0.05).

Figure 6: Effects of spike encoder order (input noise measured as the coefficient of variation, CoV) on decoding performance in the full-hand grasp (FG) task (wrist at 90◦, elbow extended). (A–B) Distribution of the coefficient of determination (𝑅2) and Pearson correlation coefficient (𝜌) for the population group, respectively. (C) A temporal comparison of the predictions and the true signal for a single randomly selected participant’s middle finger metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint angle under three spike encoder (SE) orders (𝑆𝐸𝑥 digits represent the CoV). (D) A single randomly selected participant’s evolution of the L1 loss function (𝐿𝑜𝑠𝑠𝑀𝐴𝐸 , mean absolute error) during training for the 𝑆𝐸𝑥 . * denotes statistically significant differences (𝑝 <0.05).

Figure 7: Effect of excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance on decoding performance in the full-hand grasp (FG) task (wrist at 90◦, elbow extended). WB indicates there was no restriction in the balance for the initialization and training of synaptic weights. (A) Coefficient of determination (𝑅2) for the different E/I configurations. (B) Pearson correlation coefficient (𝜌) for the different E/I configurations. (C) Mean and 95% confidence intervals of the percentage of excitatory (positive) and inhibitory (negative) first-layer synaptic weights after training. (D) The evolution of the L1 loss function (𝐿𝑜𝑠𝑠𝑀𝐴𝐸 , mean absolute error) during training for a single randomly selected participant under each balance condition. (E–F) Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint angles of the index finger for each E/I balance, showing predictions and the ground-truth signal for a single randomly selected participant.

Figure 8: Comparison of the proposed method (𝑆𝑁𝑁𝑃ℎ𝑦𝑠𝑖𝑜, labeled Ours) performance with all baseline methods. Each panel represents one of the evaluated performance metrics: (A) coefficient of determination (𝑅2), (B) Pearson correlation coefficient (𝜌), (C) maximum cross-correlation (𝑋𝐶𝑚𝑎𝑥), (D) root mean square error (RMSE), (E) mean absolute error (MAE), and (F) cross-correlation lag (𝐿𝑎𝑔𝑋𝐶 ). Values correspond to the median across the 30 conditions for each participant. * indicates statistically significant differences between 𝑆𝑁𝑁𝑃ℎ𝑦𝑠𝑖𝑜 and the baseline methods indicated by each bracket. MLP: multilayer perceptron; RR: ridge regression; KNN: k-nearest neighbors; HGB: histogram-based gradient boosting; SVR: support vector regressor; CNN: convolutional neural network.

Table 1: Performance of 𝑆𝑁𝑁𝑃ℎ𝑦𝑠𝑖𝑜 and the baseline methods. Values are the median (top) and interquartile range (IQR; bottom) across participants (n = 23), computed from the median across the 30 conditions for each participant. 𝑅2: coefficient of determination; 𝜌: Pearson correlation coefficient; 𝑋𝐶𝑚𝑎𝑥 : maximum cross-correlation; RMSE: root mean square error; MAE: mean absolute error; 𝐿𝑎𝑔𝑋𝐶 : cross-correlation lag; MLP: multilayer perceptron; RR: ridge regression; KNN: k-nearest neighbors; HGB: histogram-based gradient boosting; SVR: support vector regressor; CNN: convolutional neural network.

Figure 9: Firing properties of 𝑆𝑁𝑁𝑃ℎ𝑦𝑠𝑖𝑜 as a function of task (one-finger pinch, 1FP; two-finger pinch, 2FP; and full-hand grasp, FG) in the conditions with extended elbow and 90◦ wrist posture. (A) Smoothed composite spike train (sCST) of layer 1 (L1, gray, right axis) and layer 2 (L2, orange, left axis) over time in the test set for each task (line style), averaged across participants. (B–C) Boxplots of population firing rate by task for layer 1 and layer 2, respectively. (D–F) Inter-spike interval (ISI) distributions for each task for a representative participant, separated by layer (L1: solid gray; L2: dashed orange). (G–J) Statistical properties of the ISIs for layer 1: mean ISI, coefficient of variation (CoV), skewness, and kurtosis, respectively. (K–N) Corresponding statistical properties for layer 2. In (B–C) and (G–N), boxplots summarize one value per participant (n = 23), averaged across neurons. * denotes statistically significant differences (𝑝 <0.05).
